entries.meaning: Praise called out to a dog — or to a person you are cheering on — at the exact moment they do the thing you wanted. It is warm and a little rough, and aimed at an adult by someone who outranks them it can sound condescending.
examples: "Atta boy!" he said, scratching the retriever behind the ears.
She dropped the ball at his feet and he laughed. "Atta girl."
Atta boy — you sat the whole time without moving.
The old dog finally climbed into the truck bed. "Attaboy, Duke."
He hit the free throw and the whole bench yelled, "Atta boy!"
entries.русский: молодец!, так держать! — похвала собаке или тому, кого подбадривают
entries.variants: attaboy, atta girl, attagirl, that's a boy

entries.meaning: The standard scolding for a dog caught doing something forbidden. It is delivered low and flat rather than shouted, and it usually follows a sharp "No!"
examples: "Bad dog! Get off the couch."
He came home to shredded mail all down the hallway. "Oh, bad dog."
Bad girl — we do not dig in the flower beds.
"No! Bad dog," she said, pulling the sock out of his mouth.
Trainers will tell you that a "bad dog" three hours after the fact means nothing to the animal.
entries.русский: фу!, плохая собака! — выговор псу, застигнутому за запретным
entries.variants: bad boy, bad girl, bad kitty, no bad dog

entries.meaning: The basic recall command, and the first thing most American dogs are taught. It is said once, firmly, with the dog's name in front of it, and it is an order rather than an invitation.
examples: "Bella, come!"
He whistled twice and shouted, "Come!"
Come here, buddy — you're getting a bath whether you like it or not.
She practiced "come" with a treat in her fist for twenty minutes a day.
"C'mere," he said, patting his knee, and the puppy skidded across the kitchen floor.
entries.русский: ко мне! — основная команда подзыва собаки
entries.variants: come here, c'mere, come on
entries.see also: here boy, heel, sit, come on

entries.meaning: Two commands in one syllable: get all the way to the floor, or get off me. "Down, boy" is also said jokingly to a person who is getting overexcited about something.
examples: "Down. Good. Stay."
The Lab put both paws on her chest and her husband yelled, "Down!"
Down, boy — she isn't going to want a muddy hello.
He gets "sit" every time, but "down" takes him a second.
"Down, boy," she teased when he started in about the new truck.
entries.русский: лежать!; вниз, фу! — команда лечь или не прыгать на человека
entries.variants: lie down, down boy, get down

entries.meaning: Told to a dog with something in its mouth — a ball, a shoe, a dead bird. Said to a person, the same two words mean stop talking about this, which is a much sharper thing.
examples: "Drop it. Drop it! Good boy."
He had half a bagel in his jaws before I could get out "drop it."
Drop it, Rex. That is not yours.
She holds the tug rope until he hears "drop it," and then she throws it again.
"Drop it," the officer told the shepherd, and the padded sleeve hit the mat.
entries.русский: брось!, отдай! — собаке выплюнуть предмет; человеку — «хватит об этом»
entries.variants: drop, give, drop it now

entries.meaning: A calming word said in a long, low voice to a spooked horse or an overexcited dog. The vowel gets stretched — the sound is doing as much work as the word.
examples: "Easy, girl. Easy." He kept one hand flat on the mare's neck.
Easy now. Nobody's going to hurt you.
The dog's hackles went up and she said, quietly, "Easy."
He talked the whole time he was saddling her: "Easy, easy, there we go."
Easy, boy, it's just the vacuum.
entries.русский: тише, спокойно — протяжно, чтобы успокоить испуганную лошадь или собаку
entries.variants: easy boy, easy now, easy there, whoa easy

entries.meaning: Go get the thing I just threw and bring it back. It doubles as the name of the game, so Americans say "playing fetch" at least as often as they say the command.
examples: He threw the stick across the yard and yelled, "Fetch!"
"Fetch, girl!"
Fetch — go on, get it.
She has never once understood fetch; she just watches the ball go by.
"Go fetch," he said, and the spaniel was already in the water.
entries.русский: апорт! — принеси брошенное; заодно название самой игры
entries.variants: go fetch, fetch it, fetch it up

entries.meaning: The all-purpose reward phrase for a dog, said in a high sing-song voice that matters more than the words do. Said to an adult it is patronizing, and said to a child it lands as either sweet or sarcastic depending on the child's age.
examples: "Good boy! Yes you are!"
She scratched his ears. "Who's a good girl? You are."
Good dog — that is exactly what I wanted.
He gets a treat and a "good boy" every time he rings the bell by the door.
"Good boy," his brother said flatly when he finally took the trash out.
entries.русский: хороший мальчик, молодец — похвала собаке; взрослому звучит снисходительно
entries.variants: good girl, good dog, who's a good boy, goooood boy

entries.meaning: Walk at my side and stay there. It is the command that separates a trained dog from one that drags its owner down the sidewalk.
examples: "Heel," she said, and the shepherd tucked in beside her knee.
He can't hold a heel for more than a block before he starts pulling.
Heel! We are not chasing that squirrel.
The instructor had us walk the whole ring saying "heel" at every corner.
"Heel, buddy — there's a car coming."
entries.русский: рядом! — команда собаке идти у ноги
entries.variants: heel up, to heel

entries.meaning: A friendly summons to a dog, softer than the trained command "come." Strangers use it constantly, because they do not know the dog's name.
examples: He crouched down and slapped his thigh. "Here, boy!"
Here, girl — come see what I've got.
"Here boy, here boy," the kid called from the end of the driveway.
She whistled, then tried "here, boy," and finally went for the treat bag.
Here, boy! Come on. That's it.
entries.русский: ко мне, песик! — дружеский зов собаки, мягче выученной команды come
entries.variants: here girl, here boy here boy, c'mere boy
entries.see also: come, here kitty kitty, atta boy

entries.meaning: The standard American way to call a cat: the word kitty repeated in a high, coaxing voice, usually mixed with clicks or kissing noises. Cats generally ignore it, which everyone knows and everyone does anyway.
examples: "Here, kitty kitty kitty!" she called into the crawl space.
He shook the food bag and went, "Kitty kitty kitty?"
Here kitty — come on, it's freezing out here.
They walked the whole block after dark calling, "Here kitty kitty."
The vet tech opened the carrier door. "Kitty kitty. Nobody's going to hurt you."
entries.русский: кис-кис-кис — обычный американский способ подзывать кошку
entries.variants: kitty kitty, kitty kitty kitty, here kitty

entries.meaning: Do not touch that in the first place — the command that comes before "drop it." Dog owners use it constantly on walks, mostly about chicken bones and other dogs.
examples: "Leave it," he said as they passed the half-eaten burrito on the curb.
Leave it! Leave it. Good.
She teaches "leave it" with a treat under her shoe.
"Leave it, Moose," and to my amazement, he left it.
Leave it — that's a skunk, not a cat.
entries.русский: нельзя!, не трогай! — собаке не подбирать; предупреждение до «брось»
entries.variants: leave, leave it alone

entries.respell: PUSS-puss (the vowel of put, not of bus)
entries.meaning: An older way of calling a cat, heard now mostly from grandparents and in old books. Be careful with the longer form: pussy is vulgar slang in modern American English, so here kitty kitty is the safe choice.
examples: "Puss puss puss," my grandmother used to call from the back porch.
He set the saucer down and said softly, "Here, puss."
Puss puss — where have you been all night?
Nobody under sixty says "puss puss" to a cat anymore.
She still calls him "puss," and he answers to it about half the time.
entries.русский: кис-кис — устар. зов кошки; полная форма pussy сегодня груб. сленг
entries.variants: puss puss puss, here puss, pussy pussy
entries.see also: here kitty kitty, here boy, scat

entries.meaning: Set the dog on someone — attack. In real life it is rare and serious; in ordinary speech it is nearly always a joke about turning somebody loose on an opponent, a customer service line, or a rival team.
examples: "Sic 'em, boy!" the farmer yelled, and the dog took off after the coyote.
He pointed at the mailman and said, "Sic 'em," and the beagle wagged her tail.
Send the lawyers in. Sic 'em.
"Sic 'em!" is a Baylor thing — you'll hear the whole stadium do it.
She forwarded the email to her boss with two words: sic 'em.
entries.русский: фас! — натравить собаку; обычно шутл. «давай, задай им»
entries.variants: sic him, sic her, sic 'em boy, sick 'em

entries.meaning: The first command almost every American dog learns. Said to a person, a bare "Sit." is an order from someone with authority — a coach, a cop, a parent — and it lands hard.
examples: "Sit. Good boy."
He holds the treat over the dog's nose and says "sit," and the tail hits the floor.
Sit! Sit. We are not opening this door until you sit.
She can do sit and shake, but stay is still a work in progress.
"Sit," the coach said, and forty kids dropped onto the gym floor.
entries.русский: сидеть! — команда собаке; человеку — резкий приказ от старшего
entries.variants: sit down, sit boy, siddown

entries.meaning: A trick command telling a dog to bark once. It is taught for fun and turns up in the same breath as "shake" and "roll over."
examples: "Speak!" The terrier let out one sharp bark and got a biscuit.
He'll do sit, stay, and speak, but he will not fetch.
Speak, boy. Come on — speak.
My uncle taught his dog to speak, and now the dog barks at him about everything.
"Speak," she said, and the dog just stared at her.
entries.русский: голос! — команда собаке гавкнуть, цирковой трюк
entries.variants: speak boy, say please

entries.meaning: Hold that position until I release you. Owners stretch the vowel out and hold a flat palm forward, and the word usually gets repeated while they walk backwards away from the dog.
examples: "Sit. Staaay. Good."
He put the bowl down and made her stay for three whole seconds.
Stay — I'll be right back.
She can hold a stay across the entire yard now.
"Stay," he told the dog outside the store, and hooked the leash to the bike rack.
entries.русский: ждать!, стоять! — команда собаке не сходить с места до разрешения
entries.variants: staaay, stay there, stay put

entries.meaning: What you say to bring chickens running, usually while scattering feed. It is said fast and high, and the birds learn the sound rather than the word.
examples: "Chick chick chick!" she called, swinging the coffee can of scratch.
Here chick chick — breakfast.
He goes out at dawn and the whole flock comes at the first "chick chick."
Chick chick chick chick — get out of the road, you idiots.
My grandmother could empty the barn with one "chick chick chick."
entries.русский: цып-цып-цып — диал. так подзывают кур, обычно рассыпая корм
entries.variants: chick chick chick, here chick chick, chickie chickie
entries.see also: sooey, cluck cluck, here kitty kitty

entries.meaning: An imitation of a hen rather than a real call — said to chickens the way people talk to any animal, and said about people to mean fussy, disapproving chatter. If you actually want the birds to come, the call is chick chick.
examples: She leaned over the fence going, "Cluck cluck, ladies."
The kid ran through the coop yelling "cluck cluck" and scattered every hen in it.
Cluck cluck — anybody laid me an egg today?
The neighbors have been cluck-clucking about our fence for a month.
He made a little cluck cluck noise and the hens ignored him completely.
entries.русский: ко-ко-ко — подражание курице; о людях — ворчливое осуждение
entries.variants: cluck, cluck-cluck

entries.meaning: The soft rolling sound a pigeon or a dove makes, and by extension the noise adults make over a baby. As an interjection it is more written than shouted — you are likelier to meet the verb, as in "she cooed at him."
examples: "Coo, coo," the boy said to the pigeons, holding out a crust.
Coo — coo — came from the eaves all morning.
Everybody leaned over the bassinet going coo, coo.
She cooed at the baby until he finally smiled.
A dove landed on the rail and gave one long coo.
entries.русский: гуль-гуль, воркование — звук голубя; также умильное сюсюканье над младенцем
entries.variants: coo coo, coo-coo

entries.meaning: Turn right — the teamster's word, used for horses, mules, oxen, and sled dogs. Its opposite is haw, and a person who "doesn't know gee from haw" is hopeless.
examples: "Gee!" he called, and the mule swung the plow to the right.
Gee — gee, now — take the fork by the barn.
The musher shouted "Gee!" and the whole team leaned into the turn.
My grandfather drove a team on nothing but gee, haw, and whoa.
He can't tell gee from haw, and he sure can't back a trailer.
entries.русский: направо! — диал. окрик погонщика лошадям, волам, ездовым собакам
entries.variants: gee up, gee haw, gee now

entries.meaning: Get moving, said to a horse — a worn-down version of "get up." Americans use it constantly as a joke to hurry a person or a car along, and children shout it while riding a grown-up's back.
examples: He shook the reins. "Giddyup."
Giddy up, horsey! Faster!
The light turned green and the guy behind us leaned on the horn. Giddyup.
"Giddyap," she said, and the old gelding started walking.
We have a plane to catch, people. Giddyup.
entries.русский: но!, пошёл! — окрик, чтобы лошадь тронулась; шутл. человеку «шевелись»
entries.variants: giddy up, giddyap, giddy-up, git up

entries.meaning: Turn left — the mirror image of gee, used with draft animals and dog teams. It is a working word; nobody says it outside a field, a trail, or a joke about not knowing your left from your right.
examples: "Haw!" and the team cut left around the stump.
Gee for right, haw for left — that's the whole vocabulary.
He called haw a beat too late and put the sled in a snowbank.
Haw, haw now, easy.
The old man drove oxen with gee and haw until the day he died.
entries.русский: налево! — диал. окрик погонщика, зеркальная пара к gee
entries.variants: haw there, gee haw, haw now

entries.meaning: An old driver's call meaning stop or hold, now almost entirely replaced by whoa. It survives in fixed phrases like land ho and westward ho, and inside heave ho. Warning: standing alone in modern American slang, ho is an insulting word for a woman, so do not use it loose.
examples: "Ho! Ho there," the teamster called, and the wagon rolled to a stop.
Land ho! — the oldest shout in the language of sailing.
Westward ho, everybody. Get in the van.
He raised a hand. "Ho, now. Let's not get ahead of ourselves."
In old novels the driver says "ho" where a modern rider would say "whoa."
entries.русский: тпру!, стой! — устар. окрик остановки; отдельно ho в сленге груб. «шлюха»
entries.variants: ho there, whoa ho, land ho, westward ho

entries.meaning: A short barked syllable that marks a beat — the marching cadence, a jump cue for a horse or a dog, and a coach's word for "move." It carries rhythm rather than meaning.
examples: "Hup, two, three, four," the drill sergeant called.
She tapped the horse's flank at the fence: "Hup!"
Hup! Hup! Let's go, let's go, everybody up.
He held the hoop out and said "hup," and the dog sailed through it.
The squad went by chanting hup-two-three-four the whole length of the block.
entries.русский: оп!, раз-два! — отрывистый счёт в строю и команда на прыжок
entries.variants: hup two, hup two three four, hup hup

entries.meaning: The shouted syllable a rider uses to drive a horse into a run, usually with a slap of the reins. It has no settled spelling — you will see it written a dozen ways in Westerns.
examples: "Hyah!" he shouted, and the horse broke into a gallop.
Hyah! Hyah! Get up there!
She slapped the reins across his neck and yelled, "Yah!"
In every Western the hero says exactly one thing to his horse: hyah.
Hyah — come on, girl, we're losing daylight.
entries.русский: но-о!, пшёл! — крик всадника, посылающего лошадь в галоп
entries.variants: yah, ya, heeyah, hee-yah

entries.meaning: The word everyone thinks sled-dog drivers shout to start the team. Real mushers mostly say hike or all right, but mush gave English the words musher and mushing, so it is the one the public knows.
examples: "Mush!" he yelled, and the sled jerked forward.
Every kid who has seen one movie about Alaska yells "mush" at the dogs.
Mush on! We've got twelve miles to the checkpoint.
She says "hike," not "mush" — nobody out on the trail says mush.
He gave the runners a push and called, "All right — mush!"
entries.русский: вперёд! — окрик каюра ездовым собакам (сами каюры говорят hike)
entries.variants: mush on, mush you huskies, hike

entries.meaning: The hog call: a long "sooo" pulled up into "-ee," used to bring pigs to the trough and, in Arkansas, to bring a stadium to its feet. It is shouted at full volume with the first syllable held for several seconds.
examples: "Soooo-ee! Pig pig pig!" he hollered from the fence line.
Sooey! Come on — dinner.
Woo, pig, sooie — you'll hear sixty thousand people do it in Fayetteville.
My uncle could call hogs two fields away with one sooey.
She let out a sooey at the family reunion and three cousins answered.
entries.русский: чух-чух-чух! — диал. протяжный клич, которым созывают свиней к кормушке
entries.variants: soo-ee, sooie, pig pig pig, woo pig sooie
entries.see also: chick chick, come and get it, here boy

entries.ipa: /ǀ/ or /ǁ/ — a tongue click rather than an ordinary English word
entries.respell: tisk /tɪsk/ when the spelling is read out loud
entries.meaning: A click of the tongue. Doubled and aimed at a person it means disapproval; made once or twice at the side of the mouth and aimed at a horse it means walk on. They are two different clicks, and horse people rarely bother spelling theirs at all.
examples: She clicked twice — tsk, tsk — and the mare moved off at a walk.
He looked at the report card and went, "Tsk. Tsk."
Two quick clicks, a squeeze of the legs, and he was trotting.
Tsk tsk — and here I thought you were the responsible one.
Riders click at their horses the way drivers honk: constantly, and without thinking about it.
entries.русский: ц-ц-ц, ай-яй-яй — цоканье языком: удвоенное — осуждение, одиночное — лошади «шагом»
entries.variants: tsk tsk, tch, tut, tut-tut

entries.meaning: Stop — the universal American call to a horse, said low and drawn out. Off the horse it has become one of the most common interjections in the language, meaning "slow down," "back up a second," or plain astonishment.
examples: "Whoa. Whoa, girl." He pulled back gently on the reins.
Whoa there — nobody said anything about paying for it today.
He hit the brakes. "Whoa!"
Whoa, Nelly. Let's start that sentence over.
The horse ignored "whoa" completely and went straight for the water trough.
entries.русский: тпру! — остановить лошадь; в речи «стоп, погоди» или удивлённое «ого»
entries.variants: woah, whoa there, whoa Nelly, whoa boy

entries.meaning: A rural, drawled "get" used to drive an animal — or an unwanted person — away. It is Southern and Western in flavor, and it sounds deliberately country when city people use it.
examples: "Git!" he said, stamping his boot, and the raccoon went over the fence.
Go on, git — shoo.
Git on out of my garden, you fool dog.
He waved his hat at the steers. "Git along, now."
She told the guy selling windows to git, and he got.
entries.русский: пшёл вон! — диал. южн., прогнать животное или незваного человека
entries.variants: git on, git out, git along, go on git

entries.meaning: Go away — said mostly to cats, and to children in a mock-stern voice. It is short and sharp and almost never actually angry.
examples: "Scat!" she said, and the cat jumped off the counter.
Scat, you two — I'm trying to get dinner made.
He flapped a dish towel at the tabby. "Go on. Scat."
Scat! That's the third time you've been on that table.
The old tom did not scat; he just looked at her.
entries.русский: брысь! — прогнать кошку, а шутливо-строго и детей
entries.variants: scat now, go on scat

entries.meaning: Get out of here, said to people rather than animals. It has a 1940s gangster-movie flavor now, so Americans use it half in fun — at kids underfoot, at a friend who is hanging around too long.
examples: "Scram, kid. The grown-ups are talking."
He heard the sirens and told everybody to scram.
Scram! Before I call your mother.
She jerked a thumb at the door. "All right, you two — scram."
Nobody says scram with a straight face anymore, which is exactly why it's funny.
entries.русский: проваливай!, кыш отсюда! — людям; с привкусом старого гангстерского кино
entries.variants: scram outta here, beat it

entries.meaning: The standard word for waving an animal away — flies, birds, a cat on the counter, a dog under the table. Used on people it is playful and slightly bossy, the way an aunt clears kids out of a kitchen.
examples: "Shoo! Shoo!" She waved both arms at the pigeons.
Shoo, fly — I'm eating here.
He shooed the cat off the keyboard for the fourth time that morning.
Shoo, you two. Go play outside.
The mare swished her tail to shoo the flies off her back.
entries.русский: кыш! — отогнать муху, птицу, кошку; людям — шутливо-командно
entries.variants: shoo shoo, shoo fly, shoo now

entries.meaning: Said to a baby or toddler at the end of a bottle, a snack, or a game, usually with both palms turned up. It is the standard American way of announcing that something has finished to someone too young to be told.
examples: She tipped the empty cup toward him. "All gone!"
All gone — see? No more crackers.
He held out both hands and said, "All done, all gone," and the baby laughed.
"Cookie?" "All gone, sweetheart."
The bath drained out and Grandma sang, "Aaaall gone."
entries.русский: всё, больше нету — малышу, что еда или игра закончились
entries.variants: all done, aaaall gone
entries.see also: num-num, open wide, here comes the airplane

entries.meaning: The nonsense sound adults make while tickling a baby under the chin or on the belly. There is no fixed spelling; the word exists to be said in a silly voice.
examples: "Coochie-coochie-coo!" he said, wiggling a finger under her chin.
She picked the baby up and went kitchy-koo until he squealed.
Coochie-coo — who's got the softest little feet?
Uncle Ray does about four minutes of coochie-coo and then hands him back.
He hates being tickled, so the coochie-coo routine lasts about two seconds.
entries.русский: у-тю-тю!, кути-кути! — бессмысленный звук, которым щекочут младенца
entries.variants: kitchy-koo, kitchy-kitchy-koo, coochie coochie coo, goochie goo, cootchie-coo

entries.meaning: The line American parents say while flying a spoonful of food toward a toddler's mouth, complete with engine noises. It is a bribe dressed up as a game.
examples: "Here comes the airplane! Neeeeoooow — open up."
Here comes the airplane, coming in for a landing.
He refuses peas unless there's an airplane involved.
"Here comes the choo-choo," she said, and the spoon went in.
My dad did the airplane thing with all four of us, and it worked on exactly one.
entries.русский: летит самолёт! — приговорка при кормлении малыша с ложки
entries.variants: here comes the choo-choo, open the hangar, airplane

entries.meaning: Baby talk for food, or for how good the food is, said while feeding a small child. Adults use nom nom the same way about their own dinner, mostly online.
examples: "Num-num time! Come sit in your chair."
Are you ready for your num-nums?
Num num num — is that good?
She calls dry cereal "num-nums" and will eat a whole box of it.
He rubbed his belly. "Num num."
entries.русский: ням-ням — детское слово о еде и о том, как она вкусна
entries.variants: num nums, nom nom, yum-yum, nummy

entries.meaning: Said to anyone whose mouth you need open — a baby with a spoonful of peas, a patient in a dentist's chair, a kid at the doctor. It is friendly and a little sing-song.
examples: "Open wide — here comes the airplane."
Open wide and say ah.
The hygienist tapped the mirror against his chin. "Nice and wide for me."
Open up, sweetie. One more bite.
He opened wide before she even got the spoon out of the jar.
entries.русский: открой ротик пошире — малышу с ложкой, у врача «скажи а-а»
entries.variants: open up, say ah, nice and wide
entries.see also: here comes the airplane, num-num, say cheese

entries.meaning: The word you say when you uncover your face in the oldest baby game there is. Adults also use it lightly to mean "I can see you" — to a child hiding badly, or in a teasing note to someone who has been caught out.
examples: "Peekaboo! I see you!"
She pulled the blanket over her head and waited. Peekaboo.
He laughed so hard at peekaboo that he got the hiccups.
Peekaboo — I can see your sneakers under the curtain, buddy.
Twenty minutes of peekaboo and the kid still isn't bored.
entries.русский: ку-ку!, а вот и я! — возглас в игре в прятки с младенцем
entries.variants: peek-a-boo, peekaboo I see you, peep-bo

entries.meaning: The child's word for the toilet and for using it. Parents say "go potty" to the dog as well, which is the standard American euphemism on a walk.
examples: "Potty time! Let's go, everybody."
Do you need to go potty before we get in the car?
Potty first, then we can read a book.
She takes the dog out, says "go potty," and stands there in the rain.
He announced "potty" at the top of his lungs in the middle of the ceremony.
entries.русский: горшок; на горшок — детское слово о туалете; собаке «сделать дела»
entries.variants: potty time, go potty, pee-pee, tinkle

entries.meaning: A goofy expansion of uh-oh, borrowed from a canned-pasta jingle and said when something small goes wrong. Adults say it to kids, and to each other when they want to make a mistake sound harmless.
examples: The milk went all over the floor. "Uh-oh spaghettios."
Uh-oh spaghettios — somebody forgot to hit save.
He looked at the dent in the bumper and said, "Uh-oh, spaghettios."
"Uh-oh spaghettios!" she sang, mopping up the juice.
Every time the printer jams my coworker says uh-oh spaghettios, and I want to scream.
entries.русский: ой-ёй-ёй, опаньки — шутливое растягивание uh-oh при мелкой оплошности
entries.variants: uh oh spaghetti-o's, uh-oh spaghetti-os

entries.meaning: Said while lifting a small child — or helping anybody up off a chair, a floor, or a curb. It turns the effort into a little song.
examples: "Upsy-daisy!" He swung her onto his shoulders.
Ups-a-daisy — into the car seat you go.
She took her father's elbow. "Okay, Dad. Upsy-daisy."
Upsy-daisy, big guy. Time for bed.
He grunted "upsadaisy" hauling the last box onto the truck.
entries.русский: оп-ля!, ап! — приговорка, когда поднимают ребёнка или помогают встать
entries.variants: ups-a-daisy, upsadaisy, upsie-daisy, up we go

entries.meaning: Baby talk for bed or bedtime. Adults say it about themselves as a joke when they are giving up on the evening.
examples: "Okay — beddy-bye. Go pick out a book."
It's past eight. Time for beddy-bye.
She fell asleep on the rug before we even got to beddy-bye.
I'm done. Beddy-bye for me.
Two more minutes, then beddy-byes, and I mean it.
entries.русский: баиньки, бай-бай — детское слово о сне и о том, что пора спать
entries.variants: beddy-byes, beddy-bye time, bye-bye time

entries.meaning: A child's word for a small cut or bruise, and by extension for a small mistake. Adults say "my boo-boo" about an error to make it sound minor and forgivable.
examples: "Show me the boo-boo. Oh, that's a big one."
She kissed his knee. "All better. No more boo-boo."
He's got a boo-boo on his elbow from the slide.
Little boo-boo on the spreadsheet — I've already fixed it.
Any boo-boo, no matter how small, requires a bandage with a dinosaur on it.
entries.русский: бо-бо — детское слово о ранке или ушибе; в переносном смысле мелкий промах
entries.variants: booboo, boo boo, ouchie

entries.meaning: A gentle order to stop crying or stop talking, said to a child, a distressed adult, or a barking dog. "Hush now" soothes; a bare "hush up" scolds.
examples: "Hush now. Hush. You're all right."
She rocked him and kept saying, "Hush, hush, hush."
Hush now — the movie's starting.
"Hush," his grandmother said, and forty years later he still hushes.
Hush now. Nobody is mad at you.
entries.русский: тише, тише; ш-ш — мягкий приказ перестать плакать или шуметь
entries.variants: hush, hush little baby, hush up, shush now

entries.meaning: A soft, sing-song goodnight, said mainly to children but also between adults who are close. It is warmer and sillier than "good night."
examples: "Nighty-night. Sleep tight."
Night-night, buddy. Love you.
She waved from the doorway. "Nighty-night, don't let the bedbugs bite."
Nighty-night — I'm going to be asleep in about four seconds.
He says night-night to every stuffed animal on the bed, one at a time.
entries.русский: спокойной ночи, баю-бай — ласковое детское прощание на ночь
entries.variants: night-night, nite-nite, nighty night, nighty-night sleep tight

entries.meaning: A thing a child is not allowed to do or touch, said as a gentle prohibition. Adults keep the word for rules at work — "that's a no-no around here" — where it makes a real policy sound almost cute.
examples: "No-no. We don't touch the stove."
The outlet is a no-no, and he knows it, and he goes for it anyway.
No-no, sweetie. Gentle hands.
Showing up late to his meetings is a big no-no.
She shook her head slowly. "No-no."
entries.русский: нельзя, бяка — детский запрет; у взрослых «так у нас не принято»
entries.variants: no no, a no-no, big no-no

entries.meaning: Said the instant a small child trips, drops something, or lands on their bottom — a way of turning a spill into a joke before the crying starts. Adults use it about their own small blunders too.
examples: He went down on the grass and she called, "Oopsy-daisy! Up you get."
Whoopsie-daisy — that whole cup went on the rug.
Oopsy-daisy. Nothing broken, nobody hurt.
She dropped a stitch. "Oops-a-daisy."
Every time he falls somebody says oopsy-daisy, so he laughs instead of screaming.
entries.русский: опаньки!, ой-ёй — когда малыш споткнулся или что-то уронил
entries.variants: oopsie-daisy, whoopsie-daisy, whoops-a-daisy, oops-a-daisy

entries.meaning: A child's word for both the pain and the injury — "I have an owie." Adults use it about tiny hurts, half-mocking themselves as they do.
examples: "Owie! My finger!"
She held up her thumb. "Owie. Kiss it."
He's got an owie on his knee that needs a fresh Band-Aid every single day.
Owie — okay, that stapler is sharper than it looks.
Any scratch under an inch long is an owie in this house.
entries.русский: бо-бо!, ай! — детское слово и о боли, и о самой ранке
entries.variants: owwie, ouchie, owie-zowie

entries.meaning: The classic sound of comforting someone who is crying, usually delivered with a pat on the back. It is genuine from a grandparent to a child and often faintly sarcastic between adults, because it admits you have nothing useful to say.
examples: "There, there. It's going to be fine."
She patted his shoulder. "There there."
There, there — cry it out, and then we'll go get ice cream.
He gave me a "there there" and went right back to his phone.
There now. Nobody is angry with you.
entries.русский: ну-ну, ничего-ничего — утешение плачущему, между взрослыми часто с иронией
entries.variants: there now, there there now, there-there

entries.meaning: The director's call that starts a take. On a real set it comes after "roll sound" and "roll camera," and everyone off a set says it as a joke to start anything at all.
examples: "Quiet, everybody. Rolling... and action."
Action! — and a whole street full of extras started walking.
He held up his phone like a slate and said, "Action."
Nobody moves until you hear action, and nobody stops until you hear cut.
Action — okay, hold, hold. Let's go again.
entries.русский: мотор! — команда режиссёра, с которой начинается дубль
entries.variants: and action, rolling... action
entries.see also: cut, say cheese, ready set go

entries.meaning: Stop filming — the director's word for the end of a take, good or bad. Off the set, "cut" means stop doing that right now, and "cut it out" is the everyday version.
examples: "Cut! Great. Let's get one more for safety."
He said cut about a second too late and the boom mic is in the shot.
Cut, cut, cut — somebody's phone is going off.
The two of them kept going after "cut," and it's the best take in the movie.
Cut it out, both of you.
entries.русский: стоп, снято! — команда режиссёра остановить съёмку; в жизни «прекрати»
entries.variants: cut cut cut, and cut, cut it out

entries.meaning: The syllable a quarterback barks to snap the football. The whole rhythm — a color, a number, then "set, hut" — is called the cadence, and the ball moves on the last hut or on hike.
examples: "Blue eighty-two! Blue eighty-two! Set — hut!"
Hut, hut, hike! And the ball went straight over his head.
He jumped early on the second hut and cost us five yards.
The kids in the yard use one word for the entire game: hut.
Down, set, hut — and the line surged forward.
entries.русский: хат! — выкрик квотербека, по которому вводят мяч в игру; эквивалента нет
entries.variants: hut hut, hut-hut-hike, hike, down set hut
entries.see also: hup, ten-hut, play ball, ready set go

entries.meaning: The starter's formula at a race: runners settle into the blocks on "on your marks," rise on "get set," and go on the gun. Swimmers get "take your marks" instead.
examples: "On your marks... get set..." — and then the gun.
On your marks, everybody. This is a real race now.
The starter said "on your mark" twice, because somebody false-started.
Take your marks — and eight swimmers folded down over the blocks.
She's fastest off the blocks; by "go" she is already half a step ahead.
entries.русский: на старт!, внимание! — формула стартёра перед забегом
entries.variants: on your mark, on your marks get set go, take your marks
entries.see also: ready set go, one two three, play ball

entries.meaning: The count that gets people moving at the same instant — lifting a couch, taking a photo, starting a song. American English has a famous ambiguity here: "on three" can mean go on the word three or right after it, and somebody always gets it wrong.
examples: "Okay — one, two, three, lift."
On three. One... two... three!
Wait — is it on three or after three?
The bandleader counted them in: "A-one, and a-two, and a-one-two-three-four."
Everybody say cheese on three. One, two, three!
entries.русский: раз, два, три! — счёт, чтобы начать одновременно: поднять, снять, запеть
entries.variants: on three, one two three lift, a-one and a-two
entries.see also: heave ho, ready set go, say cheese

entries.meaning: The everyday starting signal for a race between kids, a chore, or anything you want several people to begin at once. The formal track version is "on your marks."
examples: "Ready, set, go!" And four kids tore across the lawn.
Ready set go — last one to the car is a rotten egg.
She counted them down: ready, set, go.
We said ready set go and then nobody moved.
Ready... set... — false start. Everybody back on the line.
entries.русский: на старт, внимание, марш! — обиходный сигнал к старту
entries.variants: get set go, on your mark get set go, ready steady go
entries.see also: on your marks, one two three, hut

entries.meaning: What the person holding the camera says to make a group smile, because the word forces the mouth into one. It is so worn out that Americans now say it with a sigh, and half the time the answer is a groan.
examples: "Everybody squeeze in. Okay — say cheese!"
Say cheese, guys. One more. One more.
He said "cheese" through clenched teeth for eleven straight family photos.
Say cheese — got it. You can all stop smiling now.
Nobody says cheese anymore; they just hold the phone up and count to three.
entries.русский: улыбочку!, скажите «сы-ы-р» — команда фотографа перед снимком
entries.variants: cheese, everybody say cheese, smile
entries.see also: one two three, open wide, action

entries.meaning: "Attention" squeezed into two barked syllables, ordering soldiers to snap upright. Civilians use it as a joke when somebody important walks into the room.
examples: "Ten-hut!" Forty pairs of boots came together at once.
Atten-hut! Eyes front.
Somebody yelled ten-hut when the colonel came through the door.
He still says "ten-hut" to his kids at the breakfast table, and they still hate it.
Attention on deck — the captain's aboard.
entries.русский: смирно! — армейская команда, сжатое attention; шутл. при входе начальства
entries.variants: atten-hut, tench-hut, attention on deck

entries.meaning: The conductor's call that the train is leaving and anyone riding needs to be on it. It is one of the most recognizable work calls in American English, and it gets borrowed for anything that is about to start.
examples: "All aboard!" the conductor shouted down the platform.
All aboard — last call for the 6:15 to Chicago.
He heard "all aboard" and started running, suitcase banging against his knees.
All aboard, kids. The bus is leaving with or without you.
The conductor's "booooard!" carried the whole length of the station.
entries.русский: по вагонам! — крик проводника перед отправлением поезда
entries.variants: all aboard that's going aboard, booooard
entries.see also: last call, come and get it, next

entries.meaning: The call that food is ready, shouted at a camp, a job site, or a family kitchen. It has a chuck-wagon flavor and it is always warm.
examples: "Come and get it!" she yelled from the back door.
Soup's on — come and get it before it goes cold.
He banged a spoon on the pot lid and hollered, "Chow time!"
Come and get it, boys. Beans and cornbread, same as yesterday.
Grub's up! Grab a plate.
entries.русский: готово, налетай!, кушать подано — зов к столу
entries.variants: soup's on, chow time, grub's up, come and get it while it's hot

entries.meaning: A shouted warning that an explosion is coming — originally from mining, now standard for demolition crews, the military, and every video game with a grenade in it. People also yell it before doing anything reckless.
examples: "Fire in the hole!" Everybody got behind the truck.
He pulled the pin and shouted, "Fire in the hole!"
Fire in the hole — clear the doorway.
She dropped a roll of mints into the soda bottle and yelled fire in the hole.
The crew calls it out three times before any blast.
entries.русский: ложись, взрываю! — предупреждение о взрыве у подрывников и военных
entries.variants: fire in the hole boys

entries.meaning: Get out of the way — shouted by somebody carrying something heavy or moving fast. It comes off a ship, where the gangway is the passage, and it sounds slightly old-fashioned now outside the military.
examples: "Gangway!" he yelled, coming around the corner with a stack of trays.
Gangway — hot pan, hot pan, hot pan.
Make a hole! Medic coming through.
Somebody hollered gangway and the whole hallway flattened against the wall.
Gangway, folks. We've got a piano on this dolly.
entries.русский: дорогу!, посторонись! — крик того, кто несёт тяжёлое или спешит
entries.variants: make a hole, make way, coming through
entries.see also: heads up, look out, fire in the hole

entries.meaning: A sailor's pulling chant, said on the beat when several people haul on the same rope. As a noun, "the old heave-ho" means being thrown out or fired.
examples: "Heave... ho! Heave... ho!" The rope came in a foot at a time.
Yo-heave-ho — one more good pull and she's up.
All right, on my count. Heave!
They gave him the old heave-ho after the third missed deadline.
Heave ho, everybody. This stump is coming out today.
entries.русский: раз-два — взяли!, эй, ухнем! — матросский припев при дружной тяге каната
entries.variants: yo-heave-ho, heave-ho, heave

entries.meaning: The single word that moves a line forward, called by a cashier, a clerk, a barber, or a nurse. Said flat, it is brisk and impersonal, which is exactly what a long line needs.
examples: "Next!" The line shuffled forward one step.
Next, please. Window four.
He called next before the last guy had his wallet back in his pocket.
Next in line for the fitting room?
She waited forty minutes to hear one word: next.
entries.русский: следующий! — оклик кассира, врача, парикмахера, двигающий очередь
entries.variants: next please, next in line, next customer
entries.see also: step right up, last call, all aboard

entries.meaning: The carnival barker's call, pulling a crowd toward a booth or a show. Nobody says it seriously anymore, so it now signals "here comes a sales pitch," usually with a wink.
examples: "Step right up! Three balls for a dollar!"
Step right up, folks — the show starts in five minutes.
He spread his hands like a barker. "Step right up and behold the miracle of modern plumbing."
Step right up if you want to be the one who tells the boss.
The whole midway was step-right-ups and flashing lights.
entries.русский: подходи, налетай! — зазывала у балагана; теперь шутл. перед рекламной речью
entries.variants: step right up folks, step up, hurry hurry hurry
entries.see also: next, going once, going twice, last call

entries.meaning: The logger's shout warning everyone that a tree is falling. Off the job, Americans yell it whenever anything tall goes over — a bookshelf, a stack of boxes, a friend tipping out of a chair.
examples: "Timber!" The pine came down across the clearing.
He made the last cut and yelled timberrr.
The whole stack of pallets went over. Timber.
Timber — heads up, the ladder's going.
My uncle shouts "timber" every time he stands up out of the recliner too fast.
entries.русский: берегись, дерево!, поберегись! — крик лесоруба; шутл. когда падает что-то высокое
entries.variants: timberrr, tim-BER
entries.see also: fore, fire in the hole, look out

entries.meaning: The call that brings the next hitter to the plate in baseball. Off the field it means "you're next," usually with a little dread attached.
examples: "Batter up!" the umpire called, and the game started.
Batter up — Rodriguez is on deck.
The interviewer opened the door and said, "Batter up."
He's got three kids in Little League and he yells "batter up" in his sleep.
Batter up, batter up — let's move it along, we're losing the light.
entries.русский: отбивающий, на биту! — бейсбольный вызов; в жизни «ты следующий»
entries.variants: next batter up, batter batter

entries.meaning: The referee's order to two fighters tangled up in a clinch: let go and step back. It is also what a football huddle shouts before the team claps and lines up, and what a cop says to a scuffle — "break it up."
examples: "Break! Break, I said." The referee shoved in between them.
On three — one, two, three, break!
The huddle clapped once and yelled, "Break!"
He wouldn't break clean, and the ref took a point away.
Two bouncers came over yelling break it up.
entries.русский: брейк! — команда рефери разойтись в клинче; break it up — «а ну разошлись»
entries.variants: break it up, break clean, one two three break

entries.meaning: The sound of the bell that starts and ends a round in boxing. In ordinary talk, "ding ding ding" is what people say when somebody finally guesses right — the game-show bell.
examples: Ding ding — round three.
"Ding ding ding! We have a winner."
He was saved by the bell — ding ding, and the round was over.
Ding ding ding, you got it in one.
The announcer does his own sound effects: "And there's the ding ding."
entries.русский: динь-динь — гонг раунда в боксе; «динь-динь-динь» — «в точку, угадал!»
entries.variants: ding ding ding, ding

entries.meaning: The golfer's shout warning anyone downrange that a ball is coming their way. It is called immediately and loudly, and the polite version adds the direction.
examples: "Fore!" he shouted, watching the ball curve toward the next fairway.
Fore right! Fore right!
Somebody yelled fore and everyone on the tee box ducked.
If you don't call fore, you deserve the lecture you're about to get.
Fore — sorry, folks, that one got away from me.
entries.русский: берегись, мяч! — крик гольфиста о летящем в чью-то сторону мяче
entries.variants: fore right, fore left, foooore

entries.meaning: The umpire's call that starts a baseball game or restarts play after a stoppage. Outside the park it means "let's get on with it," or, in business talk, "cooperate."
examples: "Play ball!" The crowd roared and the first pitch went in.
The rain finally stopped around four and the umpire called play ball.
All right, everybody's here — let's play ball.
The other side wouldn't play ball on the price, so we walked.
Play ball! Two outs, nobody on.
entries.русский: игра!, начали — судейский сигнал к началу матча; в делах «пойти навстречу»
entries.variants: let's play ball

entries.meaning: The shooter's call in trap and skeet that releases the clay target. It is said sharply, and the machine throws on the word.
examples: "Pull!" The clay flew out and he broke it clean.
He settled the gun on his shoulder, took a breath, and said, "Pull."
Pull — miss. Pull — got it.
Call pull whenever you're ready; there's no rush.
She shot twenty-five straight, one "pull" at a time.
entries.русский: дай! — команда стрелка, по которой машинка выбрасывает тарелочку
entries.variants: ready... pull
entries.see also: fore, ready set go, one two three

entries.meaning: The ring announcer's order for the cornermen to clear out before a round begins. It is chiefly British; American announcers reach for it only when they want the old-fashioned formality, and otherwise just shout the round number.
examples: "Seconds out — round four!"
The stools came out of the ring the moment he called seconds out.
Seconds away, gentlemen.
You still hear "seconds out" from British announcers on the late broadcasts.
Seconds out. And there's the bell.
entries.русский: секунданты, за ринг! — устар., преим. брит. команда перед началом раунда
entries.variants: seconds away, seconds out round three

entries.meaning: The bailiff's command that everyone in a courtroom stand as the judge comes in or goes out. It is one of the few American phrases that still gets an entire room to obey instantly.
examples: "All rise. The Honorable Judge Alvarez presiding."
The bailiff said all rise and a hundred people stood up at once.
All rise — court is now in session.
Everybody knows "all rise" from television, but it's just as flat and fast in person.
All rise. ... You may be seated.
entries.русский: встать, суд идёт! — команда пристава в зале суда
entries.variants: all rise please, please rise

entries.meaning: The auctioneer's warning that the bidding is about to close. Anywhere else it is a friendly ultimatum — last chance to speak up before the decision is final.
examples: "Two hundred. Going once, going twice..."
Going once, going twice — sold to the man in the green hat.
Last slice of pizza. Going once. Going twice.
He held the gavel up. "Going, going, gone."
Going twice — anybody? All right, we're moving on.
entries.русский: раз... два... — предупреждение аукциониста, что торг вот-вот закроется
entries.variants: going once going twice sold, going going gone
entries.see also: sold, last call, step right up

entries.meaning: The bartender's announcement that this is your final chance to order before the bar stops serving. It has spread everywhere — airports, offices, potlucks, anything about to close.
examples: "Last call!" The bartender flipped the lights twice.
Last call for alcohol, everybody.
Last call on the sign-up sheet — I'm sending it in at noon.
They gave last call at 1:30 and had everyone out by two.
Last call, folks. Tab, or one more?
entries.русский: последний заказ! — объявление бармена перед закрытием
entries.variants: last call for alcohol, last call folks, closing time
entries.see also: all aboard, going once, going twice, next

entries.meaning: A judge's or a chairperson's call for a room to stop talking and behave. It is nearly always doubled or extended — "Order! Order in the court!" — and it usually arrives with a gavel.
examples: "Order! Order in the court!" The gavel came down three times.
The chair called the meeting to order at seven o'clock.
Order — I will clear this room if I have to.
He banged the gavel and shouted for order over the noise.
Order, please. We have one more item on the agenda.
entries.русский: к порядку! — призыв судьи или председателя прекратить шум
entries.variants: order in the court, order order, come to order

entries.meaning: A court crier's ancient "hear ye," said three times to open a session and still used by the Supreme Court and a few state courts. It comes from Anglo-French, and even the people who say it professionally disagree about how to pronounce it.
examples: "Oyez! Oyez! Oyez! All persons having business before the Honorable Supreme Court..."
The marshal's oyez is the first thing you hear in that courtroom.
Oyez, oyez — the town crier still opens the fair that way.
Half the lawyers there say oh-YEZ and the other half say oh-YAY.
Oyez! Draw near and give your attention.
entries.русский: слушайте!, внемлите! — юр., устар. клич судебного глашатая, троекратный
entries.variants: oyez oyez oyez, o yes

entries.meaning: The auctioneer's word ending the bidding, said as the gavel comes down. In everyday speech, "sold" means you have convinced me — the fastest way in English to say yes.
examples: "Sold! To the bidder in the back row."
Sold, for eight hundred and fifty dollars.
"There's a pool, and it's ten minutes from work." "Sold."
He said the word sold about four hundred times that afternoon.
Free food? Sold. I'm in.
entries.русский: продано! — удар молотка на аукционе; в речи «уговорил, согласен»
entries.variants: sold to the lady in red, sold American
entries.see also: going once, going twice, last call, next
